en: Record of Miscellaneous Sayings of Chan Master Fohai of Shixi, Transmitted Robe Holder;
in Response to Defense Commissioner Zhang:
I have a single field, within which I rest all myriad conditions. Though my livelihood is utterly still, my daily activities are not in vain.
Contentment brings the joy of longevity; without seeking, one dwells in meditation wherever they are. The neighbor to the west understands this intent; pine and bamboo dissolve the cold mist.
Seeing off Chan Master Chao as he returns home to visit his kin:

though he has never yet penetrated the profound mystery of the Way, he is willing to learn like the man of Xinfeng who did not return ten times out of ten. Upon returning, he recites Qingliang’s response to the Buddha: "Even if you were to grind my bones to powder, I would not return."
A discourse. To teach my daughter that there is the pivot of the Patriarchs:
Returning clouds drag other clouds as they follow the dragon away, yet return; without intention, they seem to come with intention. It is simply because I fear losing the old monk.
The door of the cave on Eternal Day Rock has not been opened for years;
the stench of the hermitage’s own sweat has never been noticed. Before his mouth has even opened, people already know; he has suffocated two stones out of Suzhou.
The Buddha—some cover their noses, others knit their brows.

Zhongshan’s heroic bearing rises a thousand fathoms above the mundane; standing like a sheer cliff, solitary and precarious, it cannot be grasped. North, south, east, and west, they labor in vain with their axes.
E: Who would have known that every step was within it? Xingxing, Hall Attendant:
Heading to Xiachuan to beg for oil, my body is cold, ashen, old, and sick.
A single lamp in the deep night accompanies this solitary poverty; I must endure these dripping tears while longing for home.
Tears. Tell this to those who inquire after your illness at the head of the stream.
Different hands, the physiognomist and the earth share the same root, returning to a single finger. "Three or four," Master—this is already too much. Casually, he raises his fist.
As for the dwelling place: how can one calculate its measure?
One who has been sent forth by Master Baohui is born into the family of the Tathāgata;
they must study the conduct of the Tathāgata. May all thoughts enter into right mindfulness, and may those with contention return to non-contention.
The Buddha-land of Shaolin is no longer seen; the great assembly at Mount Tai is worthy of reliance. Who is that person on the waves?
Who am I? Raising your eyebrows, you should take heed and reflect deeply.
Seeing off the Abbot Lin on his visit to his parents:
Ten times he did not return, yet now he returns; ten times he wished not to see me again, yet now he sees me again. The Great Way of antiquity and today is ever level and plain;
each must open up their own single thread at their own gate.
I see you off, Master Gong, for Mount Lu;
if one has not reached Mount Lu, one is no monk. These words and this speech—when have they ever truly existed? Now my inspiration is spent and I return home;
the Five Elders still lean against their ancient green peaks.
Sending off Attendant Gan: Following his original teacher back to Luchuan, he relied upon that master to inquire and investigate until there was nothing left to inquire about.

It was simply a case of calling "three" and responding with "three. When the dialogue reached the point of not being mutually辜负 (gu-fu—disappointing or failing one another), Luchuan was fundamentally the same as the old Luchuan.
The Meng Family Estate presented a verse upon sending off a monkey; I respond in kind to thank them.
Dwelling among crags and caves, you were a companion to bears and tigers; now reared at my gate, you are sent away to Stone Creek.
To understand the General’s intent in nurturing all creatures, do not let your cries disturb us as you pass to and fro.

When Yan-shou rolls up his transformation-curtain, how is it different from when he lets it down? A gentle breeze lightly stirs as the green clouds hang low. At night, the mosquitoes roar like thunder shaking the earth;
lying safely upon my sick pillow, I know nothing at all.
Shen Jian recorded his dream:
Within a single mote of dust lie three thousand worlds; in half a kṣaṇa span eighty thousand springs. Thus they come and go, thus they abide;
one knows not who is host and who is guest.
Farewell, Great Master Hui:
you have shaved your dark hair and donned the *kāṣāya*. With sutras, dharma wheels, and prayer beads always by your side, you seek to strike the profound pivot and realize your own nature.
Behold the reality of things as you visit the abode of Jueyi.
Master Chang (whose style name was Gweyeon) resided at Gwangbok-sa and spoke this verse to encourage him:
The Gweyeon-gui fragrance has long been wafting; The season now urges the opening of the field for selecting Buddhas.
Do not act like Moshan, who offered but half a ladle, Causing others to pointlessly call out, "Niang-niang!"
Master Cong’s title was Wumen.

On the day he was sent to take up residence at Guangfu Monastery, there was a great assembly for a vegetarian feast at Mount Tiantai. A phrase that transcends the physical body is beyond all contrivance; now it has fallen into the hands of Wumen.
Releasing both and gathering both—its dynamic function is peerless.
I tell you, Elder Ben:
do not wander through markets where "yu" is mistaken for "lu," or "diao" for "dao. Do not follow after those who confuse "qian" with "gan" or "shi" with "bu.
Should we have the karmic affinity to meet again in the future, this golden-maned lion must let out its roar.
I bid farewell to Daoist Master Li as he delves deeply into the five thousand characters of the *Daodejing*. Every single character is a book spoken from your own house;
if you wish to know the principle of "the mystery within mysteries," it is found in serene clarity, with nothing remaining unaccounted for.
I present this verse for the year of Guiwei;
it brings with it a matter full of paradoxes. Ten times ten, a thousand times a thousand—it is no more than that.
Meeting on a narrow path, one briefly raises a hand; look at how his eyes and mind are!
The Zen of the kitchen steward Songguang is pungent and sharp—a single flavor. How could its mastery ever reside in the ladle?
Before these fifteen hundred spiritual friends had even stepped out the door, the teaching was already complete.
When Master Zhen sent off Dai Qi, both were simultaneously set down. One should observe the reality well and visit Juzhi;
who has been entrusted with this singular splendor that has descended for five hundred years until now?
Sending the mind to its place of purity, I dwell in profound dhyāna within the realm of worldly toil. How many times has my compassionate heart been shattered and then restored?
Having let go of gain and loss, right and wrong, every single thing is the mountains and rivers of my own ancient home.
The practitioner Zhi Jiang returned to Mount Lu and requested a verse:
"The wild grass before the courtyard is lush and green; I recall again the time Danxia cleared it away.
Having met at the high peaks of the Lotus Society, Upon returning, he once more mounts the Holy Monk."
Minor Buddhist Rites (The Sequence of Ritual Procedures according to the *Bingyan Qinggui*) First:
Relocating the Coffin;
Second: Locking the Coffin; The Honored Guest Ascends the Seat.
The Great Immortal’s mind is intended for entrustment; ten thousand virtues cannot bring it forth, and a thousand hands cannot grasp it away. Elder Immortal, let it go!
Seize it with vigor! If you can enter this gate at this moment, you must still lock off the path of frantic pursuit.
The third hanging scroll:
Stonefield (Shitō) Worthy, a fragment of cloud from the Southern Mountains, a drop of water from West Lake—his true face is fully revealed; where can he be avoided?

To say it is the Elder Stonefield is to face him across a thousand miles; to say it is not the Elder Stonefield is to be a thousand miles away from him even while facing each other. Is it so? Or is it not?
(Then he unfolds the true [text] and says: It is all right here. Cease debating the extinction and arising of bubbles. Love and grasping are a pure breeze pervading the earth.
For the fourth time, the lamentation is raised:
Master Wuzu comes empty-handed and bare, yet he fills the void so completely it cannot be parted; he goes forth naked and bare, yet he piles up mountains.
"The mountain has no place to rest. Even so, this is still only for those of the initial capacity; it is not yet the final word. But what is the very last word?
(Looking at the assembly) Heaven! Heaven! What bitter suffering! What bitter suffering!
The fifth offering of tea:
Elder Tieta, at the fifth watch, his drowsy eyes were still lost in confusion. His lingering dreams had not yet reached home;

he had exhausted all medical texts and mastered every secret formula, yet it was all for the sake of this single bowl of bitter, astringent tea. It was here that Elder Zhengjue realized the very life-vein [of the Way]. Long ago—
In the Hall of Perfect Enlightenment years ago, we met yet did not meet; today before the Nirvana Platform, we part yet do not part.
Although this is so, let us respectfully drain this cup to the dregs and swiftly turn back from amidst the mass of blazing flames.
The sixth offering of hot water (missing);
the seventh, the Small Private Inspection before the Spirit:
For Master Wuji of Jingci, our school has no words or phrases, nor does it bestow a single dharma upon others. Therefore, as soon as Deshan entered the gate, he struck him with his staff. Lin...
When Jì entered the gate, he let out a shout. It was like beating a drum smeared with lethal poison; it was like pressing down the Vajra King. Those who hear it perish;
those who even intend to approach it are lost. Proceeding directly in this manner, the Way is cut off and men are desolate.
Nevertheless, though not even a needle may pass through officialdom, we cannot help but open another path. Two thousand years ago, ten thousand *li* away, we shall meet face-to-face in person. Ah!
Hehe. A person has come from Jiangxi reporting that Mount Jiyun at Yangshan stands shoulder-to-shoulder with Mount Lianshe at Mount Lu.
Together they traveled to Kuśinagara in Central India, arriving just on the fifteenth day of the second month, when the Yellow-Faced Old Man entered parinirvāṇa.
Lying within his golden coffin, he exposed his two feet and spoke this verse: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; this is..."
"Phenomena arise and perish; when arising and perishing have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss. Thereupon, he transformed his body into the fire of samādhi and cremated his golden-hued form.
Seeing that the diamond *śarīra* within the flames was not something for us to handle, they returned to pay their respects to the Great Master Bodhidharma at the foot of Mount Xionger.
They bowed their heads in greeting, but upon raising their eyes to look, the Great Master was already beyond the Pamir Mountains, carrying a single sandal in his hand.
He was walking alone, striding with ease. [Nanyue] stepped forward and asked, "Why is your pace so hurried? I would be grateful to hear a word from you. He replied, "Five people traveling together;
for ninety years, there has been neither 'self' nor 'other. Then, pointing his finger, he said, "Wu-na, the Great Master of Caoqi is packing his bags to return to Xinzhou.
You ought to go see him off. Upon hearing these words, the Great Master raised his hand and waved it back and forth.
He said: "Leaves fall and return to their root; when coming, there was no mouth. This provoked the Elder of Infinite South Mountain (Nanshan Wujie Lao Ren), who could not restrain his amusement.
He took up his brush and wrote a verse: "Sixty-four years, I have loathed Buddhas and patriarchs. With a single laugh, I turn my body— Empty space is revealed alone.
Thereupon, he rode backward upon the Pavilion of the Wisdom Sun, exited through the main gate, crossed West Lake, and departed into the distance, solitary and serene. (He lets out a shout.)
Jiyun Peak returns to Mount Gui; Lianshe Peak returns to Mount Lu. (Holding up the staff, he says:

"As for my staff here, though it does not enter their protective communities, within the way of benevolence and righteousness, it must also assist in the lamentation. (He strikes the ground once with the staff. Again, he cites:
A monk asked Nanyuan, "Where have all the sages of antiquity gone? Nanyuan said, "If they do not ascend to heaven, they enter the earth."
The monk asked, "What about you, Master? Yuan said, "Do you know where Old Baoying has fallen? The monk hesitated. Yuan struck him across the mouth with his whisk.
He then called the monk forward and said, "The order was for you to carry it out," and struck him once more with the whisk.
Xuedou said, "Since the order was carried out by himself, yet the whisk does not know its own origin. Xuedou said.
"To say 'blind' is to add frost to snow. The Master said, "To say 'it is' is to employ one's full capacity; to say 'it is not' is to rely on power to deceive others.
If you know where the Head of Jingci falls, you will know where all the sages of the past have fallen.
But where are they right now? (After a long silence, he said: "They cannot remain within the rank of Buddhas and Patriarchs; they are cut off from both the human world and the heavens."
Arrangements were made.
For the eighth [rite], the enshrinement of the coffin:
Attendant Zhen’s thunder shook the blue heavens and struck the drum of "poisoned lacquer. A sharp-witted monk nodded his head in self-assurance, taking Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa as...

The Master took Jing Mountain as his father; though he entered and exited with his fellow disciples, they were mutually disappointing one another. Since you already know that moving the step does not move the body, how could it compare to moving the body and then moving the step?
At the ninth gate, hang the portrait (missing). At the tenth gate, tea (missing).
At the eleventh gate, hot water (missing).
At the twelfth, extinguish the fires. The Guest Master shall oversee this.
Zhaozhou offers tea; Shaoyang draws a glance. Shitian reveals his local sentiments to the core; with a single hand, he hands everything over at once.
He thus exchanges South Mountain for North Mountain and shifts Eastern Land to Western Land. Discerning guest, wake up and take heed! Take another step forward:
before your feet have even crossed the mountain of blades, you cast yourself into the great mass of fire.
Master Wujie of Jingci [Temple], the second torch-bearer (with a verse).
Holding up a torch, he said: "This torch-handle has already been fully explained by the Lecturer of Upper Zhusi. I, Lingyin, cannot help but add a head atop a head.
For sixty-four years, my transgressions have filled the heavens; I have harbored a deep hatred for the Buddhas and Patriarchs. He then tied [the knot].
Exhausting all resentment and suffering, with a single laugh he turns his body around; kicking over the painted vase, empty space is revealed alone.
To go on in this manner—this was the final personal entrustment of Master Wuji, yet it is not the phrase of his ultimate total manifestation.
A stone liver and intestines, an iron mask—before even ascending the mountain of knives, one first throws oneself into the mass of fire.
To cause the Iron Ox of Shanfu to swallow the Stone Tiger of the South Mountain—even this is not yet the master’s display of appearing and disappearing, rolling up and unrolling, his playful sport.
The Old Man of Infinite reaches a certain level of genuine excellence that words cannot reach; how can it be discussed? (Throws [the staff])
(Torch Cloud) Apply it here. The thirteenth, the Elder Coolness and Formlessness: he holds up his robe and says, "The entire earth is the true essence of coolness;
there is not a single thread that is not the wondrous garment of formlessness. This robe cannot...

To conceal [one's faults]—how could the Heavenly Peace (Tianning) possibly lift this up? (Raising his robe, he says: "Beneath Mount Kukkuṭapāda, before the Many-Son Stupa, its breadth and length are perfectly proportioned and exact.
If you can take responsibility for this, it will not only be of great value to the Sahā world;
were you to hesitate, it would be worth five hundred pieces of gold for a single proclamation."
The fourteenth announcement:
The secondary hall is located beside the Geyang Bridge, where the two monasteries meet. Outside the gates, there is a stretch of vacant land where water and clouds gather.
Since you have been told that there are sacred relics here, it is as well to let the blind donkeys follow the herd. Do you wish to see them? The masks are present right now.
Master Zhantang: "The very place where the bone enters is eternally tranquil;
though you seek it, it cannot be seen. Do you wish to see it? (Holding up the bone, he says: "This is Master Zhantang."
It was toward the place where flying stars scatter fire that it was gathered up and fell into the hands of this mountain monk. How, in the end, shall it be disposed of?
Master Zhantang, in a place where the sun and moon do not reach, you must perform an urgent somersault.
The fifteenth was Abbot Yuan. He entered the stupa having come from Jianmen.
He had long resided at Nanhu Temple; he was said to be the same as Nanhu, yet not merely comparable to Nanhu.
He rides astride the three-legged donkey of Yangqi; how many times has he sold yellow millet in the market towns?
With a Buddha’s mouth and a serpent’s heart, a chicken’s head and a phoenix’s tail—all at once brought into this gate. The scenic splendor of the pagoda doors belongs entirely to you.
Supervisor Yuan, you should understand this well; do not fall asleep in the cold of your own neglect.
The sixteenth, Master Chijue: Before entering the Patriarchs’ Hall and ascending Mount Zhongfu Aranya, he had already occupied the Lingxiao Stūpa. Do not say that this old man has no fixed abode;
it is simply because of poverty that one laments having too many bodies. Thus it is, thus it is. Let go and look at the two manifestations in their respective places. Not so.
"Is it so? Or is it not? At noon, it remains as before, lacking half its light.
This is the thirty-fifth abbot of this mountain, Zen Master Chijue; where now shall he be placed? Do not say there is no rank for him;
where would he not be honored? (The above concerns the funeral rites for the incumbent abbot; the sequence is as follows.)

Venerable Yuet-ting. Do you remember the first step taken by Venerable Yuet-ting of Bao’en in Danqiu before the second torch was lit? At that initial moment, the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai nodded his head unconsciously;
at that final opportunity, the Elder of Miaofeng has been scratching his forehead in anticipation until this day. It is thus.
"Ma! A single fragment of solitary radiance should be known by itself. Not so, not so—dividing the brilliance in two places is to lose one's purity.
Regarding this coming and going of birth and death, today we let it all pass at once. (Holding up the fire, he said:
"Master Yuetting, this very thing cannot be called 'the true emptiness of the nature-fire,' nor can it be called 'the true fire of the nature-emptiness. Directly—"
Accepting this with humility, listen attentively as White Cloud provides the essential breakthrough.
For Tandu, who once served as the master of the estate, the ancestral fields and gardens were already fully known; at midnight, neither person nor ox was present.
I see. This is precisely the time of moonlight. (A certain person): Do not pursue the final word. For seventy-five years, there has been a shadowless tree;
now behold the branches being drawn back from within the fire.

The Head Cook (the lower fire) uses a *yeli* for the soup and a wooden ladle for the rice. For two years, they share the same spring. Thus, one should diligently attend to the affairs according to the Dharma.
Within this mountain community, there are sixty mouths; the old cook relies solely upon this single point. What is this single point? [Name].
Do you understand? A spark flies from the bottom of the great ocean; how does it compare to Pòzào Duò of Mount Song?
(To the Head Seat, while performing the cremation:
Solitary and beyond all grasping, carefree and without dependence. For forty-four years, [he was like] Bèibí of Fángtán. Second in the Celestial Palace.

While I was sitting on the seat preaching the Dharma, my eyes were not yet open from sleep. At Jingshan, you sat on the seat beside me to uphold the essential principles of our school; those words are still ringing in my ears.
(Name), let us set aside all other matters for now. Now that the wind has just subsided and the rain has just cleared, as you depart without any further business, accept this monk’s torch.
Master Yuxi (extinguishing the funeral pyre):
Coming thus from Mount Huilang, dwelling thus at the eaves of Tiansheng, and departing thus from the summit of Lingxiao Peak—[Name], the weather is cold;
come here and warm yourself by the fire.
The Venerable Qian was the abbot; Gu knew the storehouse; De-li served as the head of the workmen.
Entering the stupa, the affairs of the world were as blazing as a mass of fire; the old Qian understood them all completely.
Now, changing his step and shifting his body, he departs—this is precisely the moment the lotus blooms and the Buddha is seen.
Profound, firm, obscure, and remote; only those who reach it know its subtle workings. Only by being firm do you know the treasury; the whole body resides herein.
Amidst green mountains and white clouds, within purple mists and crimson flames—scattered fires and flying stars are all there for you.
There is virtue that can be established; there is no Way that can be cultivated. When asked about matters in the field, he folds his hands and drags the spade.

His true nature being thus revealed, his ugliness is difficult to conceal. (So-and-so) has his back to the mountain in the shade and faces the place where the sun shines; meeting many children, he laughs without ceasing.
Regarding Xitang’s (extinguishing the funeral pyre):
Does the Elder Yue’eng of Xiangfu still remember? Thirty years ago, he was born with an iron mask.

Turning his feet toward Simeng River, he tramples the path across the Simeng River. He does not lean upon the walls and fences of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, nor does he enter the gates of Laozi and Zhuangzi.
Dwelling at Xiangfu, he does not act as the master of Xiangfu; relying on Lingxiao, he does not act as a companion to Lingxiao.
Amidst the bubbling harmony of the *ou-ou* and the firm knots of the *kuang-liu*, he abides in a state of pure joy.
Vast and indistinct. Now that the clouds have dispersed and the waters have flowed away, where else would you go?
[The person] has not yet ascended the mountain of knives, but has already climbed the mass of fire.
The Abbot of Gan-yuan (with a verse): Zhen Xiu-zao (performed the cremation) at sixty-four years of age.
Dense and continuous, following the square and pursuing the circle, he lost one half. The clouds gather and the rain disperses.

The iron boat has reached the shore; the moon sets into the blue sky. His face and features remain as they were before. In the river country, the spring wind blows through the second and third months;

in the flower and tree groves of the Brocade Capital, the blossoms vie for their loveliness. The Abbot of Gan Monastery drew a circle and said: "What is it like when this very thing suddenly comes into operation?
He then tossed up a torch and said: "Just keep watching!"
Chan Master Zhen of Jian Pass achieved great spiritual efficacy: when he acted, even a swan’s feather was light; when his work was complete, even a mountain was heavy.
Thus, for thirty years, he assisted Master Fojian in the construction of this monastery. Yet, while he shared in Fojian’s realization, he did not share in his common worldly ties.
In this "Great Enlightenment" chamber of mine, the labor and materials were measured by the public office; yet who would have expected that the time would come so suddenly for him to depart forever?

He was diligent in his practice and construction projects. After long rains, when the weather was about to clear but had not yet done so, he would remain there, cherishing the search for the seeds of fire.

As the Master of the Mountain, his virtue was profound and his status eminent; his insight was clear and penetrating. Having studied with devotion during his youth and exerted himself to serve his teachers, he resided [in this position] in his later years.

Ascending the mountain, he responded to circumstances with spontaneous transformation. To manifest the sacred traces of the Venerable Golden Buddha, he conjured forth palaces of jade and halls of crystal.

One day, his merit was perfected and his fruition fulfilled; with a resonant entrustment, he departed. Yet he still left behind a single stalk of thatch from after the fire, requiring Jing Mountain to pass judgment.
(Lifting up the bone, he says: "Master Sheng, you cannot gather it though you embrace it, nor disperse it though you brush it away. Let it lie in disarray by the side of the empty cliff."
Secretary Kang (performing the cremation):
From west to east, from east to west—every step is entirely it; every step is also not it. While you are alert and mindful, you may remember the time of arriving home;
yet those three hundred poems from before have here become nothing more than empty effort. Let go from within emptiness; do not think any further.
Listen! A stone man atop the ridge sings a song; the golden Buddha crossing the furnace raises its brows.
Fazen, the head monk (who performs the cremation), is a true son within the chamber of Shuangjing;
how could he be like a wanderer outside the gate? Step by step is one’s own mountain; thought after thought is all...
Right Concentration. At times one relinquishes the pure to enter the defiled; at times one removes the defiled to maintain the pure.

Abiding in neither extreme, yet not dwelling in either extreme—this is non-discursive proliferation that ultimately transcends all proliferation. When the Dharma reaches the pinnacle of purity, the youths Bing and Ding invite you, wishing for you to speak of some Zen ailment.
Manager Yu, Master An, and Master Zhen (who manages the cremation):
Manager Yu, from east to west of the stream and from end to end of the fields, you send forth and gather back, leaving nothing wasted.
Supporting [the work] in this way and maintaining such a standard, the principal and interest will both be realized; do not covet a full measure of profit. Manager Yu, look on with cool detachment.
Now, what a fiery color this is!
The Master of the Stūpa, the Master of the Stūpa—the mountain monk shall also offer a turning word: how does it compare? The golden-haired lion within the cave.
A fierce tiger dwelling in the forest possesses a majestic and awe-inspiring presence; yet its claws and fangs have never been bared for eighty years.

Though one searches for it, there is no place to be found. That which cannot be found is precisely where it dwells. Master of the Pagoda, now, amidst this mass of blazing flames, you must exert your utmost spirit and seize the opportunity for yourself.
The meeting of teacher and disciple: three calls and three responses. (Holding up the torch, he says: Relying solely upon this, the entire Great Canon is brought forth and entered.
(Holding up the torch, he says: Relying likewise upon this, the Buddhas of the three periods turn the Great Dharma Wheel upon the flames.
But what do you rely upon? O Master of the Precious Treasury, exert your spirit; do not let it slip away.
Master Chao bathes; the Head Monk Shao (Stone-Field Junior Master) is the first water-server (extinguishing the fire).
Neither washing away dust nor washing the body, the wondrous touch is proclaimed and made clear, and one dwells as a child of the Buddha.

You may know only that which is peaceful and secure in the middle way, yet you have not yet realized that there is no place for cold in the cauldron of boiling water. Master Chao, do you understand? The flame—!
To take up the mantle within the inner chambers.
(The person) wishes to know the master’s household? To inherit it is very easy; to sustain it is most difficult.

Sustaining it is still relatively easy, but guarding it is what is truly difficult—difficult indeed! When the walls and roof are both crumbling, it is difficult; when the pure breeze sweeps the ground, it is easy. To inherit...
The Monastery Administrator: Do you understand? Before every door, torches burn;
the rain falls in drops, the wind whistles through the air. The vines wither and the trees fall, so I shall compose my mind to retire from the world.
Since you know how to strike the ice to preserve the seeds of fire, what prevents you from stirring the embers to find the floating bubbles?
Vice-Abbot Hyang (performing the cremation): Hyang (pronounced with the *xù* rhyme; meaning "jade").
Originally there was no birth, and now likewise there is no extinction. When it is time to act, one simply acts—how truly marvelous!
Selling Dongshan’s ginger in two places, yet throughout his life employing the secret instructions of Shaolin. Vice-Abbot Hyang, at the end, you were thus so earnest. If...
May the mountain monk take up the torch to assist with the warmth.
Master Yi, Hall Master, and Vinaya Master Qing (extinguish the fire).

In this ancient hall where there is no Buddha, incense smoke rises day after day and lamps burn night after night. From where does this sacred sound come? It must surely be the true essence of Shaolin.
Planting grass may be called performing a meaningful task; this is the awakened mind. What words are these? Performing meaningless tasks is the distracted mind;
what words are these? Master Yidian: neither being nor non-being constrain him.
With body and mind vast and open, he remains just as he is; yet he comes forth from within the fire to manifest a lotus flower.
The principle of pure emptiness: its essence is suchness (*tathatā*). To have it is to impair one’s virtue; to lack it is to lose one’s body. Whence comes it? Whither goes it?
Who is near? Who is distant? (Name of person): Vast and empty, let all be cast aside;
beneath a blazing sky, snow falls as one embraces a red furnace.
Master Yuanjue (Qiling), from the ground of non-abiding, manifested a body with form.
Having dwelt among humans for sixty-nine years, he realized hundreds of thousands of samādhis within a dream.
His pure land is the mind alone; though he manifested coming and going, he did not fall into coming and going. He was Amitābha as his own nature, fully endowed with all virtues.
Having perfected *Avalokiteśvara-bodhi*, he abides in the maintenance of *Avalokiteśvara-bodhi*. He speaks of precepts, concentration, and wisdom to adorn his own person;
he employs neither emptiness, nor the provisional, nor the Middle Way to guide future students. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he is always within this state.

Though it is said that he was granted the Golden Terrace, he thoroughly understood that the myriad dharmas are not received. When his tasks were completed, he folded his robes and departed; shifting his body and changing his step, he went forth.
How would you express this? Not far from here, before the Terrace of Nirvāṇa, there is a spiritual friend named the Brahmin Jvalanāditya;
you should go there and inquire.
Master Tong’an, as you covered your remains with earth, you realized that within the sameness of all phenomena there is difference; all things were blended together within a single hermitage.

Now, having cast aside both sameness and difference, you have trod upon the highest peak of the flying mountain. We respectfully pay our respects to the newly passed away Great Lecturer, the Chief Registrar of Tong’an.
The Master arrived through the power of compassionate vows; his arrival was from nowhere. He abides by means of compassionate vows; his abiding is without a fixed location.

Therefore, from the root of non-abiding, he manifests the efficacy of conditioned phenomena. Adorning his own person with precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom, he points toward emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way for the benefit of later students.
The teaching tradition relies upon him. Although his seat has been moved many times, it is said that there is a Way to be transmitted—like a scaled fish in brocade.

It was like stagnant water; in truth, there was no Dharma to be preached. Like a painted phoenix soaring through the clouds, within the mere blink of an eye during his sixty-nine years, he remained composed in speech and laughter as he rolled up his robes and departed.
Beyond the clouds, the celestial fragrance suddenly grew silent; amidst the seats, the rain of flowers was instantly strewn in disarray.
All thought that when the land of Wu by the river ended, it was the end of the world; who would have known that beyond the opposite bank lay so many mountains of Yue? At this—
If you wish to see the Elder Tong’an, it will not suffice merely to look here. Do you want to see the Elder Tong’an?
You cannot find him within the niche of Fulong; yet you encounter him amidst the shadows of white clouds.
The Goryeo lecturer opened the coffin;
his beard and locks were like iron chains locking the azure sky. The chains snapped, yet the path of flight remained impassable.
Cherish you, O guests of non-action and non-affair, who do not realize that the whole body is contained therein. Thus, I, Huiyin Zhengzhu, the direct successor of Xianshou, [speak] from Goryeo.
The lecturer in the hall was not somber; for seventy-three years, he has been fundamentally without coming or going. Hundreds of thousands of samādhis are constantly manifest before him.

His advancing and retreating, his every step and stride, are entirely the realm of the Great Man of the Middle Way. His speech and silence, his movement and stillness, are none other than the Dharma-gate of the wondrous principle of true emptiness.
Everywhere he moves like an elephant king turning in circles; at every point, he displays the vigorous prowess of a lion. Thus it is.
So it is. Let us cease discussing the moon at midday upon the terrace; whether it be so or not, let it be. And as for the possibility that Mount Sumeru might fall to the earth—let it be as it may.
At this very moment, tell me: when the Master of the Unabiding Monastery constantly dwells within it, yet does not linger upon even a single phrase of it, what then?
The golden lock of the profound gate is snapped in two; the great thousand-fold world-system’s scripture emerges from a single speck of dust.
When the donor smelts the hair (applying fire from below), there remains but a single hair-tip;
this very hair-tip blinds the eye at the crown of the head. Eradicate it and leave nothing behind.
This very tip of a single hair is not merely a tip of a single hair; it is like mountains piled high and vast peaks, filling the valleys and filling the ditches.
Each and every one of these tips of a hair—whether they are indeed tips of a hair or not—is likewise so. If you understand this, you will see that amidst the blazing flames, snowflakes fly.
There is no need to sweep away the flames to seek the śarīra.

The Practitioner recites the Dharma Jewel (and performs the cremation).
The supreme treasure within the Way—where can it be sought? Seeking it internally and externally, no trace is found; yet in daily life, its use is perfectly appropriate.
For thirty-three years, he was the son of the Chen family, yet he did not inherit his ancestral lineage’s occupation. At four, five, or six years of age, he left home at Tianning Monastery;
he did not weed the grass before the hall, nor was he bound by birth and death or coming and going, nor did he concern himself with *bodhi*.
This is a source of affliction. Nevertheless, one must further know that there is a final phrase. As it is said:
"To those who pass through this barrier, I entrust it with a single hand."
For the sake of wisdom, he recited the Five Precepts (the lower fire).
At Tiantai Lín-hǎi, he recited the Five Precepts. In the hall of Lingyin, how many years have passed? Sweeping the floor and replenishing the incense burner is his new livelihood;
gathering firewood and providing water is his old way of life. He does not worry that robes and alms bowls have not come into his hands; rather, he rejoices that body and mind are already [at peace].
Leaving the household life (reciting the five precepts). Amidst the blazing conflagration of the kalpa-fire, there is no turning back. Return to receive a single kashaya robe;

one who knows how to manage the rice-head (extinguishing the fire) and settle the affairs of leaving the household is a true renunciant. To sift the rice and discard the grit is not it; to sift the grit and discard the rice—that is it.
Nor is it so. (Raising the firebrand, he says: "For his sake, let these few sparks be ignited; let them fly as embers throughout the world.
(He extinguishes the fire. The pure path and the pure person:

leaving home requires diligent effort and the preciousness of refined cultivation. Food and clothing should be taken according to one's lot; do not seek them elsewhere. [The verse continues: "A stone falls at the waist; greed for treading..."
The millstone. Unaware that the bright moon has passed over the Cangzhou isles; since you have become a guest within the halls of Lingyin, you ought to take Master Lu as your model.
If you do not clarify the mind and realize its nature, it will be as if it never happened, and you shall inevitably be tormented by the suffering of birth and death.
This year, he followed me to Tiger Hill; a lingering illness bound him, and he simply ceased to be. He has ceased, indeed he has ceased—but ultimately, where does he go?
Go! Take this mountain monk’s torch; going clearly and coming clearly, one may wander at ease.

the wind-driven birds shake the sea, white waves overturn the sky; they do not covet the fragrant bait in the deep, azure pool.
Holding the broom, he comes to the garden; (the fire below) is in the Lingyin Hall for guests.
To attend to the garden, he brings the broom; the hoe-head is lightly raised and cast down. This matter is entirely free from doubt or conjecture.
Understanding how to grasp the Bodhi tree, plant it everywhere within the fire. Come to the garden head; do not add more wood to the ashes in the furnace.
Though the iron tree has no flowers, they shall nonetheless bloom.
For Old Man Zhu (the cremation):
The Four Ming Mountains of Eastern Zhejiang; the waters of West Lake in Western Zhejiang. If you wish to know the face and features of Old Man Zhu, they are simply these very things.

Throughout his life, his wondrous function and spiritual powers were foremost in transporting rice and carrying firewood. Having endured sixty-six hardships, his heart in serving his master was fundamentally unlike others’.
When people said he was dead, how could he truly be dead? I say he emerged from that state and has not yet returned here.
I present you with this single,浑仑 (undifferentiated) phrase as you go: before the door of every house is a torch.
For Lady Yu of the Zhang Family: the coffin is raised, and the earth is covered.
The formless body and the body with form—how many times has the golden palace been renewed? Looking back over a hundred years, it is all but a dream.
Who is the one who remains lucid while dreaming? Lady Yu, the deceased, passed away after forty-nine years. From [the beginning]... there was none.
Born from within forms, one enters extinction within forms;

in the interval, whether moving or still, speaking or silent, coming and going upon the golden palace and before the white jade tower—all such wealth, nobility, and splendor are nothing other than Buddha-work.
One must know that within a dream there is that which does not dream. An ancient said: "The physical body perishes and decays; what is the indestructible Dharma-body? He replied: "Mountains."
The flowers bloom like brocade; the mountain stream is as clear as indigo. If you can comprehend this, there is no hindrance to walking hand-in-hand with the Seven Sages’ Daughters.
Should you hesitate, then listen to this verse: Within the vast expanse of dust, a gathering of the seven treasures—this is not yet the place where one may find rest.
Amidst the shadows of the green mountains, white clouds drift by; take your time, shifting your steps.
Hasten back!
Before the world was yet formed, this plot of land already existed. Once the womb was prepared, it belonged to Lady Yu.

Now that the earth has opened and the heavens have unfolded, the splendor overflows the eyes; mountains encircle it and waters wind around it, and the spirit of spring fills the foreground. It is precisely at this moment...
At the hour of interment, how could one suddenly bear the grief of parting? The Palace Attendant comforted him as they parted; the son bowed in farewell.
The relatives were crushed with sorrow, unable to detain him even as he departed.

At such a time, people only know that the Lady’s jade has been buried here, yet they do not know that for a Son of the Buddha, dwelling in this very place is the very enjoyment of the Buddha. Furthermore, who is this Son of the Buddha? And what is he called?
How do you act upon this ground? Within it, one receives and uses [all things], walking, pacing, sitting, and reclining—all are contained therein.
The Buddha-land and the heavenly realms do not dwell outside the mind. As for the final phrase, how is it? A single mote of dust completely shields and protects all.
Wealth, honor, and glory are left to future generations.

Guo Gong, as you rise from the coffin and the earth is covered over, birth arises from within the formless, and extinction transforms and perishes within the realm of forms. Within this, the mind-consciousness is fundamentally...
Emptiness. A single point of spiritual radiance constantly shines through all. The late Mr. Guo Si has seen it thus: originally he did not come;
like a tiger crouching and a dragon coiling, every face is opened wide. Now he likewise does not go; the waters of Wu and the Qinhuai River remain just as they are.
Serene and unclouded, it responds to the movements of coming and going; to whom has this singular splendor been entrusted?
What a fine moment for a turning—this green mountain has waited long beyond the clouds.
Among these, there is one treasury of yellow gold. For how many years has it been hemmed in by snow and buried by clouds? The splendor before one’s eyes is boundlessly fine;
now, truly, to whom does it belong? It belongs to Guogong—do you see it? The mountains of Huai stand upright, the great river comes to pay court;
pines and vines surround it, mists and clouds unfurl and fold. O worthy father and elder brother, sixty years...
To behold their faces once more—who was first and who was last? O fine descendants, you are the concentrated essence of five hundred years of flourishing vitality.

Richness and nobility may truly be called the place where the family lineage rests; the dwelling where one finds peace in the Nine Graveyards. Leaves fall and return to the root; forgetting the self, one attains the essential meaning.
How can the final word be proclaimed? With eyes open or closed, it is the Western Land. To raise [the staff]: [The staff is raised.]**
May your feet find ultimate bliss.
Having served as an official under the Shanghai Cai Prefecture, you have now raised the spirit-tablet for your departure;

holding the torch, you ride upon a single leaf of a boat, drifting with the tide across shallow and deep waters. Seeking the ford at Shanghai, you visit Sanlin, where you encounter me amidst the reflections of water and clouds.
The earth—ten thousand *li* of level fields are but a single mind. Thus, I, a subordinate official of Lord Cai, came here in former days;
I have lived here for my entire life. It was here that I managed my livelihood and established my career; it was here that I served those above and raised those below.

Even when I broke down the fences to widely distribute benevolence and practiced the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) by traveling across all the mountains, I never departed from this place. This is so.

His fields and gardens were so vast that crows could not fly across them; his descendants were as numerous as a dense forest, filling the space before him like a flight of geese, yet none ever departed from this place.
How marvelous, how marvelous! How rare, how rare! His noble deeds were but just completed at the age of eighty-one spring seasons.
He brushed off his robes and returned to the West; it has already been two hundred and sixty days. For what reason do the tides carry a mournful sound and the wind’s melody hold such sorrow?
As he approaches the site of cremation, fragrance drifts upon the water—this is precisely the moment when the lotus blooms; there is no regret regarding life and death.
But as for this "one move" of turning back around—how is that? At the head of the Double Cypress Hermitage, a promise was once made; wait and see within the flames.
Manifesting the Udumbara flower.
